title: fubar: a fast, unconstrained bayesian approximation for inferring selection
display_name: FUBAR: A Fast, Unconstrained Bayesian AppRoximation for Inferring Selection
abstract: model-based analyses of natural selection often categorize sites into a relatively small number of site classes. forcing each site to belong to one of these classes places unrealistic constraints on the distribution of selection parameters, which can result in misleading inference due to model misspecification. we present an approximate hierarchical bayesian method using a markov chain monte carlo (mcmc) routine that ensures robustness against model misspecification by averaging over a large number of predefined site classes. this leaves the distribution of selection parameters essentially unconstrained, and also allows sites experiencing positive and purifying selection to be identified orders of magnitude faster than by existing methods. we demonstrate that popular random effects likelihood methods can produce misleading results when sites assigned to the same site class experience different levels of positive or purifying selection--an unavoidable scenario when using a small number of site classes. our fast unconstrained bayesian approximation (fubar) is unaffected by this problem, while achieving higher power than existing unconstrained (fixed effects likelihood) methods. the speed advantage of fubar allows us to analyze larger data sets than other methods: we illustrate this on a large influenza hemagglutinin data set (3,142 sequences). fubar is available as a batch file within the latest hyphy distribution (http://www.hyphy.org), as well as on the datamonkey web server (http://www.datamonkey.org/).

title: work related stress, burnout, job satisfaction and general health of nurses
display_name: Work Related Stress, Burnout, Job Satisfaction and General Health of Nurses
abstract: gaps in research focusing on work related stress, burnout, job satisfaction and general health of nurses is evident within developing contexts like south africa. this study identified the relationship between work related stress, burnout, job satisfaction and general health of nurses. a total of 1200 nurses from four hospitals were invited to participate in this cross-sectional study (75% response rate). participants completed five questionnaires and multiple linear regression analysis was used to determine significant relationships between variables. staff issues are best associated with burnout as well as job satisfaction. burnout explained the highest amount of variance in mental health of nurses. these are known to compromise productivity and performance, as well as affect the quality of patient care. issues, such as security risks in the workplace, affect job satisfaction and health of nurses. although this is more salient to developing contexts it is important in developing strategies and intervention programs towards improving nurse and patient related outcomes.

title: slicing up global value chains
display_name: Slicing Up Global Value Chains

authorships.name: Robert Stehrer
institutions: Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies

abstract: in this paper, we slice up the global value chain using a decomposition technique that has recently become feasible due to the development of the world input-output database. we trace the value added by all labor and capital that is directly and indirectly needed for the production of final manufacturing goods. the production systems of these goods are highly prone to international fragmentation as many stages can be undertaken in any country with little variation in quality. we seek to establish a series of facts concerning the global fragmentation of production that can serve as a starting point for future analysis. we describe four major trends. first, international fragmentation, as measured by the foreign value-added content of production, has rapidly increased since the early 1990s. second, in most global value chains there is a strong shift towards value being added by capital and high-skilled labor, and away from less-skilled labor. third, within global value chains, advanced nations increasingly specialize in activities carried out by high-skilled workers. fourth, emerging economies surprisingly specialize in capital-intensive activities.

title: why not a world city? astana, ankara, and geopolitical scripts in urban networks
display_name: Why Not a World City? Astana, Ankara, and Geopolitical Scripts in Urban Networks
abstract: abstract the world cities literature typically examines how and why certain cities achieve world city status, but this article examines why some actors eschew the world city competition and choose not to engage the discourse, despite deploying the very same urban development tactics. through a case study of astana, kazakhstan's new capital city, i argue that state- and nation-building concerns in the era of independence have prevailed over interests in engaging the free market and liberalist narratives that accompany the world cities discourse. demonstrating how the nazarbayev regime has largely modeled its astana project on atat rk's development of ankara, i jointly examine geopolitical discourses that shape how the relationship between the two cities is narrated and interpreted by elite and ordinary citizens alike. drawing on data from interviews, focus groups, and participant observation conducted in kazakhstan from 2009 2011, i demonstrate how these identities support the nazarbayev regime's state-dominated economic arrangements much more effectively than could a neoliberal world cities script. [keywords: kazakhstan, turkey, capital city, world cities, comparative urbanism, geopolitics.]

title: conquistadors, monsters, and maps: moby-dick in a new world context
display_name: Conquistadors, Monsters, and Maps:Moby-Dickin a New World Context
abstract: abstractherman melville's moby-dick (1851) is read within a hemispheric american context of transmission across political and cultural borders. a reinterpretation is proposed of what many still regard as the 'great american novel' by examining the national concerns of moby-dick in relation to a longer new world history of european conquest and settlement in america, north and south. inter-american hieroglyphic and cartographic sources are identified for the novel and the argument is made that, by redeploying colonial print and visual archives that form the legacy of new world writers, melville reverses the course of jacksonian nation-building, which was rapidly making the us the political successor of the spanish empire and was likely to replicate its recent failures.keywords: archiveamericasconquesthemispheremelvillemoby-dicknew world additional informationnotes on contributorsantonio barrenecheaantonio barrenechea is assistant professor of english at the university of mary washington. his forthcoming publications include an article on herbert e. bolton and interamerican intellectual history for a special issue of comparative literature titled 'the americas, otherwise'. he is currently completing 'america unbound: hemispheric legacies in the postwar encyclopedic novel', a book-length manuscript that examines the incorporation of colonial new world archives in contemporary north american fi ction.

title: medical technology into healthcare and society. a sociology of devices, innovation and governance
display_name: Medical technology into healthcare and society. A sociology of devices, innovation and governance
abstract: faulkner, a. medical technology into healthcare and society. a sociology of devices, innovation and governance . hampshire : palgrave macmillan , 2009 238 pp. 50 isbn 13-978-0-230-00171-8 (hbk ) yes, another book about the conundrum of health technology and society! alex faulkner, of the institute of society, health and ethics at cardiff university, has decided to defy his mother s advice. in his book s dedication, faulkner tells us that she saw no point in conundrums , while his father liked them. perhaps together they formed the perfect paradoxical environment for nurturing a scholar of a unique mind, one that has learned to examine the relationship between health technology and society pragmatically, without ever losing track of why and how this conundrum matters. drawing on several years of empirical research experience, faulkner has now given us a broad-ranging scholarly analysis of a topic that will never cease to fascinate and challenge modern societies. through its content and structure, this book successfully achieves several objectives. it builds on five detailed case studies of different kinds of medical technology, rigorously analysed in a comprehensive framework which sheds light on their specific innovation pathways. the case studies include: artificial hips, the prostate specific antigen (psa) test for prostate cancer, infusion pumps, coagulometers and tissue engineering. these were chosen because they exemplify a range of configurations of technology-healthcare system-evidence-regulation-users. this comparative case study primarily focuses on the uk and europe and largely draws on qualitative interviews and document analysis. within these changing european contexts, faulkner scrutinises how new social dynamics, regulatory regimes and governance systems that capitalise heavily on evidentiality have contributed to forge varying innovation pathways. faulkner s comparative empirical approach to health technology definitely represents one key asset of the book. the devices he is examining are the locus of a host of social, economic and medical interests. controversies abound and the evidence-based medicine movement that has gained worldwide momentum provides one salient strategy in the form of health technology assessment (hta) to help regulate the use of healthcare innovations. nevertheless, as shown by faulkner s case studies, the struggles for defining the right kind of evidence and incorporating it into policymaking are far from straightforward. from a theoretical standpoint, faulkner s book brings a significant contribution to the current literature on health technology and society. his own approach is strongly inspired by the social shaping of health technology framework in which social actors are seen as influencing the goals, forms and features of innovations in the early phases of their development and use. it goes further, however, by drawing more extensively on the way various users (physicians, patients, regulators acting on behalf of society) negotiate what innovations should be achieving and why, and on the concept of heterogeneous engineering which faulkner redefines in order to bring forward the interdependence between various actors and the power imbalances at play. by doing so, not only faulkner pays more attention to the structural forces that are shaping innovations, but his analyses of the regulatory regimes and governance schemes associated to various devices also become more salient and instructive. his approach thus gives more teeth to the co-construction of technology and society framework and makes his book closer to blume s (1992) study on medical imaging devices in his book insight and industry in whish relationships between the state, medical insurers and medical groups were paramount. of course, faulkner does, like other academics, coin new terms that are meant to describe the empirical world better. first, usership of technologies is used throughout the book and defines the way in which technologies become embedded in everyday professional and patient practices, their social meanings and their implications for social organization in the workplace and elsewhere (p.19). this term provides more insights into the interface between the design of health technologies and their social use than did the notions of the configuration of users and of domestication. the former was very well articulated in various chapters in oudshoorn and pinch s book how users matter (2003) where some authors argued in favour of abandoning the distinction between design and use, while the latter was clearly illustrated and expanded upon in hyysalo s dissertation users of innovation (2004) in which he examines how and when users engagement does or does not contribute to technology redesign. perhaps the concept of usership will succeed in bringing more coherence to what happens when health technologies become socially embedded, without blurring the boundaries between design processes and real-world usages. the second term coined by faulkner is governation, which suggests the mixture of governance and innovation to be observed in the process of regulatory policymaking (p.161). this term specifically emerges from his case study on tissue engineering, where it is used to indicate the constructive, inventive action of stakeholders in the european regulatory state in shaping the boundaries and rules of engagement for that piece [tissue engineering] of the evolving jigsaw puzzle of technological healthcare (p.201). whether this concept will prove useful in future science, technology and society studies remains debatable. although it does aptly capture a significant phenomenon in the current conundrum of regulatory practices and the emerging hybrid technologies (in the field of biotechnology in particular), its ability to inform how regulatory regimes and evidentiality operate in the case of established technologies where there is a need to build on precedents rather than innovate may be limited. the concluding chapter of faulkner s book is brilliantly structured. it first offers a summary of the five case studies that are exemplars of the major trends characterising modern healthcare systems. the notions explored include the intensification of the workplace, the implantability and biocompatibility of new technologies, the amplification of risk, the citizen-patient empowerment movements and the privatisation taking place within public welfare systems. the chapter then provides broader observations that challenge how the co-construction of technology and society framework and other sts concepts have been applied so far. this discussion will be extremely instructive to graduate students and scholars who are seeking to understand the relationships between health technology, evidence, regulation, health policy and society and the fact that not all technologies are interpretively flexible to the same extent. of particular interest is faulkner s discussion about the processes of medicalisation and de-medicalisation that are associated with innovations. hence, despite some passages that may appear lengthy and sometimes too detailed, this book is well executed. its focus on how design, usership and regulatory frameworks interact makes it unique. it represents a worthwhile supplement to other books recently published in the field.
